items.stem: Which of the following best describes "limitation"?
options: The reason a source was created and its intended audience, which shapes what it includes and omits
Information, often biased or misleading, deliberately spread to promote a political cause or point of view
Accurate, relevant information from the candidate’s study that is not contained in the sources
The ways in which a source’s origin, purpose or content reduce its usefulness for a specific enquiry
items.answer: The ways in which a source’s origin, purpose or content reduce its usefulness for a specific enquiry
items.markingKey: D. "limitation" is the ways in which a source’s origin, purpose or content reduce its usefulness for a specific enquiry.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "Primary sources are always more valuable than secondary sources." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Value depends on the enquiry; a secondary source can be more valuable because it draws on many primary sources with hindsight.
items.markingKey: Value depends on the enquiry; a secondary source can be more valuable because it draws on many primary sources with hindsight. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a primary source and a secondary source.
items.answer: A primary source was produced at or close to the time by participants or witnesses; a secondary source is a later interpretation, usually by a historian using primary sources.
items.markingKey: A primary source was produced at or close to the time by participants or witnesses; a secondary source is a later interpretation, usually by a historian using primary sources. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using President Kennedy’s televised address of 22 October 1962 as an example, explain the influence of purpose on a source’s value.
items.answer: Kennedy announced the discovery of Soviet missile sites in Cuba and a naval “quarantine” of the island. Its public purpose was to justify the quarantine and rally US and allied opinion, so it reveals official US justifications but conceals the secret debate in ExComm.
items.markingKey: Context (Kennedy announced the discovery of Soviet missile sites in Cuba and a naval “quarantine” of the island.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Its public purpose was to justify the quarantine and rally US and allied opinion, so it reveals official US justifications but conceals the secret debate in ExComm. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the influence of purpose on a source’s value.

items.stem: Using the ExComm tapes secretly recorded in the White House in October 1962 as an example, explain how a source’s origin can increase its value.
items.answer: Kennedy recorded meetings of his advisers; transcripts were released in the 1990s. Because participants did not expect publication, the recordings reveal real options considered (air strike, invasion, blockade) and are more candid than public speeches.
items.markingKey: Context (Kennedy recorded meetings of his advisers; transcripts were released in the 1990s.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem:
Source A: Nikita Khrushchev, Soviet leader, private letter to President Kennedy, 26 October 1962 (extract)

If there is no intention to tighten that knot and thereby to doom the world to the catastrophe of thermonuclear war, then let us not only relax the forces pulling on the ends of the rope, let us take measures to untie that knot.

Assess the usefulness of Source A to an historian investigating the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, referring to who produced it, when, why and what it contains.
items.answer: Value: A private letter between leaders, it reveals Soviet willingness to compromise and Khrushchev’s fear of nuclear war at the crisis’s peak. Limitations: It was written to influence Kennedy, so it presents the USSR as peace-seeking and does not explain why the missiles were deployed; it is translated and gives only one moment in a fast-changing crisis.
items.markingKey: Value: A private letter between leaders, it reveals Soviet willingness to compromise and Khrushchev’s fear of nuclear war at the crisis’s peak. Limitations: It was written to influence Kennedy, so it presents the USSR as peace-seeking and does not explain why the missiles were deployed; it is translated and gives only one moment in a fast-changing crisis. items.stem:
Source A: President John F. Kennedy, televised address to the American people, 22 October 1962 (extract)

Within the past week, unmistakable evidence has established the fact that a series of offensive missile sites is now in preparation on that imprisoned island. The purpose of these bases can be none other than to provide a nuclear strike capability against the Western Hemisphere.

Source B: Nikita Khrushchev, Soviet leader, private letter to President Kennedy, 26 October 1962 (extract)

If there is no intention to tighten that knot and thereby to doom the world to the catastrophe of thermonuclear war, then let us not only relax the forces pulling on the ends of the rope, let us take measures to untie that knot.

Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree that the Cuban Missile Crisis was resolved mainly because of Kennedy’s skilful crisis management?
items.answer: Kennedy’s management mattered, but the settlement depended on compromise by both leaders.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – supporting: choice of quarantine over air strike; use of ExComm to weigh options; secret back-channel through Robert Kennedy and Dobrynin. Challenging: Khrushchev’s decision to withdraw missiles; secret US undertaking to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey; mutual fear of nuclear war. Judgement: Kennedy’s management mattered, but the settlement depended on compromise by both leaders. items.stem: Explain why value and limitations must always be judged in relation to a specific enquiry.
items.answer: Usefulness is not fixed: a propaganda poster is a poor source for what happened but valuable evidence of how a regime wanted to be seen.

items.stem: Hana writes: "The message of a speech is the same as a summary of everything it says." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The message is the key argument or intention; a summary of content without identifying the point being made does not explain the message.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the content of a source and the message of a source.
items.answer: Content is what the source shows or says; the message is the point it makes, which may be implied through irony, symbolism or selection.
items.markingKey: Content is what the source shows or says; the message is the point it makes, which may be implied through irony, symbolism or selection. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to David Low’s cartoon “Rendezvous” (Evening Standard, 20 September 1939), explain how it illustrates the use of irony in a visual source.
items.answer: Hitler and Stalin bow politely to each other over the body of a dead soldier representing Poland, greeting each other as “the scum of the earth” and “the bloody assassin of the workers”. The polite gestures contrast with the insults, mocking the hypocrisy of two ideological enemies who had allied to divide Poland.

Source B: Paraphrased from V. M. Molotov, Soviet Commissar for Foreign Affairs, speech to the Supreme Soviet, 31 August 1939

The Soviet government could not wait while Britain and France delayed. The pact removes the danger of war between Germany and the USSR, and narrows the zone of possible military clashes in Europe.

With reference to both sources and your own knowledge, assess the validity of the argument that the Nazi–Soviet Pact was primarily a defensive move by Stalin.
items.answer: Stalin acted from a mix of security fears and opportunism; the secret protocol shows it was not purely defensive.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – supporting: Western appeasement at Munich excluded the USSR; Anglo-French mission to Moscow in August 1939 was low-level and slow; the USSR needed time to rearm after the purges. Challenging: secret protocol gave the USSR eastern Poland and the Baltic states; Soviet invasion of Poland on 17 September and of Finland in November 1939; opportunistic territorial expansion. Judgement: Stalin acted from a mix of security fears and opportunism; the secret protocol shows it was not purely defensive. items.answer: Both may be accurate from different perspectives, or emphasise different aspects; disagreement must be explained, not just resolved.

items.answer: Corroboration is agreement that confirms information; contradiction is disagreement that must be explained by examining the sources’ origins and purposes.

items.stem:
Source A: Neville Chamberlain, British Prime Minister, speaking from a window of 10 Downing Street, 30 September 1938

My good friends, for the second time in our history, a British Prime Minister has returned from Germany bringing peace with honour. I believe it is peace for our time. Go home and get a nice quiet sleep.

Assess the usefulness of Source A to an historian investigating the Munich Agreement of September 1938, referring to who produced it, when, why and what it contains.
items.answer: Value: It reveals the Prime Minister’s public presentation of Munich and the relief that greeted it; it was said the day after the agreement. Limitations: It was a spontaneous public statement intended to reassure a crowd; it does not reveal Chamberlain’s private doubts or the rearmament programme he continued.

items.stem: Briefly describe the debate in the House of Commons in October 1938 and explain what it reveals about how contrasting sources reveal different perspectives.
items.answer: Most MPs supported Munich, but Churchill, Duff Cooper (who resigned as First Lord of the Admiralty) and others attacked it. Speeches from the same debate show the divide between those who saw Munich as preserving peace and those who saw it as a humiliating defeat.

Source B: Winston Churchill, Conservative MP, speech in the House of Commons, 5 October 1938 (extract)

We have sustained a total and unmitigated defeat. We are in the presence of a disaster of the first magnitude. All the countries of Mitteleuropa and the Danube valley, one after another, will be drawn into the vast system of Nazi politics.

items.answer: Both agree that Munich was a decisive moment for Europe. [Cartoon] Hitler and Stalin meet over the body of a dead soldier lying on the ground (Poland). Hitler raises his cap and says: “The scum of the earth, I believe?” Stalin bows and replies: “The bloody assassin of the workers, I presume?”

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the Nazi–Soviet Pact of August 1939, considering its author, date, intended audience and content.
items.answer: Value: Published weeks after the pact and the invasion of Poland, it shows British public perceptions of the pact and its hypocrisy. Limitations: It is a satirical cartoon by an anti-fascist artist; it expresses opinion, not evidence of the leaders’ motives, and simplifies the Soviet invasion of eastern Poland on 17 September.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the debate in the House of Commons in October 1938 shows how contrasting sources reveal different perspectives.
items.answer: Most MPs supported Munich, but Churchill, Duff Cooper (who resigned as First Lord of the Admiralty) and others attacked it. Speeches from the same debate show the divide between those who saw Munich as preserving peace and those who saw it as a humiliating defeat.
items.markingKey: Context (Most MPs supported Munich, but Churchill, Duff Cooper (who resigned as First Lord of the Admiralty) and others attacked it.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Speeches from the same debate show the divide between those who saw Munich as preserving peace and those who saw it as a humiliating defeat. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how contrasting sources reveal different perspectives.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Hoare–Laval Pact of December 1935 and explain what it reveals about the failure of collective security.
items.answer: The British and French foreign ministers secretly proposed giving Italy much of Abyssinia; the plan was leaked and Hoare resigned. It showed the leading League powers were willing to reward aggression to keep Mussolini as an ally against Hitler, undermining the League’s credibility.
items.markingKey: Context (The British and French foreign ministers secretly proposed giving Italy much of Abyssinia; the plan was leaked and Hoare resigned.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It showed the leading League powers were willing to reward aggression to keep Mussolini as an ally against Hitler, undermining the League’s credibility. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the failure of collective security.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the Cuban Missile Crisis was resolved mainly because of Kennedy’s skilful crisis management.
items.answer: Kennedy’s management mattered, but the settlement depended on compromise by both leaders.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: choice of quarantine over air strike; use of ExComm to weigh options; secret back-channel through Robert Kennedy and Dobrynin. Arguments against: Khrushchev’s decision to withdraw missiles; secret US undertaking to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey; mutual fear of nuclear war. Supported judgement: Kennedy’s management mattered, but the settlement depended on compromise by both leaders.

items.stem: "The Nazi–Soviet Pact was primarily a defensive move by Stalin." Discuss.
items.answer: Stalin acted from a mix of security fears and opportunism; the secret protocol shows it was not purely defensive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Western appeasement at Munich excluded the USSR; Anglo-French mission to Moscow in August 1939 was low-level and slow; the USSR needed time to rearm after the purges. Arguments against: secret protocol gave the USSR eastern Poland and the Baltic states; Soviet invasion of Poland on 17 September and of Finland in November 1939; opportunistic territorial expansion. Supported judgement: Stalin acted from a mix of security fears and opportunism; the secret protocol shows it was not purely defensive. Markbands: Use the IB Paper 2/3 markbands, scaled to the marks: top band – clearly focused, well structured, accurate and relevant knowledge used to support critical analysis, different perspectives evaluated, reasoned conclusion; middle band – mostly accurate knowledge, some analysis but partly narrative; lower band – little understanding of the demands, mainly description.

items.stem: "The Munich Agreement was a reasonable policy given Britain’s situation in 1938." With reference to specific historical evidence, discuss the validity of this view.
items.answer: Munich was understandable in context but strategically costly; historians remain divided between orthodox criticism and revisionist sympathy.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Britain’s rearmament was incomplete, especially air defence; Dominions and public opinion opposed war; gave a year to prepare radar and fighter production; abandoned Czechoslovakia and its defences and arms industry; encouraged Hitler’s belief that the West would not fight; excluded the USSR, contributing to the Nazi–Soviet Pact. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Munich was understandable in context but strategically costly; historians remain divided between orthodox criticism and revisionist sympathy. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "purpose"?
options: The use of images or objects in a visual source to represent ideas, groups or nations
Confirming information in one source by finding agreement in another independent source
Information, often biased or misleading, deliberately spread to promote a political cause or point of view
The reason a source was created and its intended audience, which shapes what it includes and omits
items.answer: The reason a source was created and its intended audience, which shapes what it includes and omits
items.markingKey: D. "purpose" is the reason a source was created and its intended audience, which shapes what it includes and omits.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The use of images or objects in a visual source to represent ideas, groups or nations"?
items.answer: symbolism
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of symbolism.

items.stem: Explain why a compare-and-contrast answer should not simply describe each source in turn.
items.answer: End-on description leaves the comparison implicit; marks reward explicit links showing where and how the sources agree or differ.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: End-on description leaves the comparison implicit; marks reward explicit links showing where and how the sources agree or differ. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between using a source as evidence and describing what a source says.
items.answer: Using a source as evidence links its content to a point in the argument; describing it merely paraphrases its content.
items.markingKey: Using a source as evidence links its content to a point in the argument; describing it merely paraphrases its content. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a source written after the event may still be valuable.
items.answer: Hindsight, access to documents and reflection can give a broader perspective, and later memoirs reveal how participants justified their actions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Hindsight, access to documents and reflection can give a broader perspective, and later memoirs reveal how participants justified their actions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that the message of a speech is the same as a summary of everything it says. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The message is the key argument or intention; a summary of content without identifying the point being made does not explain the message.
items.markingKey: The message is the key argument or intention; a summary of content without identifying the point being made does not explain the message. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why two sources may describe the same event very differently.
items.answer: Their authors had different perspectives, purposes, audiences and access to information, as with Chamberlain and Churchill on Munich.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Their authors had different perspectives, purposes, audiences and access to information, as with Chamberlain and Churchill on Munich. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source C: Haile Selassie, Emperor of Ethiopia, address to the League of Nations Assembly, Geneva, 30 June 1936 (extract)

It is collective security: it is the very existence of the League of Nations. God and history will remember your judgment.

What does Source C suggest about the failure of the League of Nations in the 1930s? Refer closely to the source in your answer.
items.answer: The Abyssinian crisis is a test of collective security and of the League’s survival; members who fail Ethiopia will be judged by history.
items.markingKey: The Abyssinian crisis is a test of collective security and of the League’s survival; members who fail Ethiopia will be judged by history. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]. Points must come from the source itself; own knowledge is not credited in this question.

items.stem:
Source A: President John F. Kennedy, televised address to the American people, 22 October 1962 (extract)

Within the past week, unmistakable evidence has established the fact that a series of offensive missile sites is now in preparation on that imprisoned island. The purpose of these bases can be none other than to provide a nuclear strike capability against the Western Hemisphere.

An historian is researching the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962. Explain the value and limitations of Source A for this research, with reference to its origin, purpose and content.
items.answer: Value: It is an official statement by the US President at the height of the crisis, revealing the public US justification and the tone of the American response. Limitations: It is intended to persuade a domestic and international audience, so it presents Soviet aims as purely offensive and omits US missiles in Turkey and the secret deliberations.

items.stem: Using the doctored Soviet photograph of Lenin addressing troops in May 1920 as an example, explain the manipulation of photographs as propaganda.
items.answer: In later versions Trotsky and Kamenev were removed from the steps beside the platform. The alteration shows how Stalin’s regime rewrote the visual record to erase rivals, so the image is evidence of propaganda rather than of the event.
items.markingKey: Context (In later versions Trotsky and Kamenev were removed from the steps beside the platform.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The alteration shows how Stalin’s regime rewrote the visual record to erase rivals, so the image is evidence of propaganda rather than of the event. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the manipulation of photographs as propaganda.

items.stem:
Source B: Winston Churchill, Conservative MP, speech in the House of Commons, 5 October 1938 (extract)

We have sustained a total and unmitigated defeat. We are in the presence of a disaster of the first magnitude. All the countries of Mitteleuropa and the Danube valley, one after another, will be drawn into the vast system of Nazi politics.

How far can Source B be trusted as evidence for the Munich Agreement of September 1938? Refer to the origin, purpose and content of the source.
items.answer: Value: A contemporary parliamentary speech by the leading critic of appeasement; it shows the opposition to Munich. Limitations: Churchill was a political outsider seeking to discredit government policy; his later reputation means the speech is often read with hindsight; it is a minority view in 1938.

[Cartoon] Hitler and Stalin meet over the body of a dead soldier lying on the ground (Poland). Hitler raises his cap and says: “The scum of the earth, I believe?” Stalin bows and replies: “The bloody assassin of the workers, I presume?”

Source B: Paraphrased from V. M. Molotov, Soviet Commissar for Foreign Affairs, speech to the Supreme Soviet, 31 August 1939

The Soviet government could not wait while Britain and France delayed. The pact removes the danger of war between Germany and the USSR, and narrows the zone of possible military clashes in Europe.

Compare and contrast the views expressed in Source A and Source B on the Nazi–Soviet Pact of August 1939.
items.answer: Both acknowledge that the pact was a deliberate agreement between Germany and the USSR. Low presents it as a hypocritical deal whose victim is Poland, whereas Molotov presents it as a peaceful, defensive measure forced on the USSR by Britain and France; Low implies aggression, Molotov peace.
